name: Linear
tagline: Issue tracking and project planning for software teams that value focused workflows.
description: Linear is an issue-tracking and project-planning tool designed around software development workflows. It combines issues, cycles, projects, roadmaps, and developer integrations; teams should evaluate how its opinionated workflow fits their own process.
seoTitle: Linear Review 2026: Workflows, Strengths, Limits & Alternatives
seoDescription: An editorial profile of Linear covering issue tracking, cycles, projects, developer workflows, trade-offs, adoption, and alternatives.
pros: A focused issue-tracking workflow connects day-to-day work with projects and cycles.
Keyboard-driven navigation and a streamlined interface may reduce friction for teams that prefer a structured workflow.
Developer integrations can connect issues with code work when the team's repository process fits the available capabilities.
Projects and roadmaps help teams communicate planned work beyond individual issue lists.
cons: The opinionated workflow may be restrictive for teams that need highly customized processes or complex approvals.
Teams needing broad portfolio resource planning, built-in time accounting, or extensive non-engineering workflows should verify fit first.
Migration requires careful mapping of statuses, fields, projects, attachments, and historical issue relationships.

content.title: Who Linear Fits Best
content.body: Linear is worth evaluating when a product or engineering team wants a consistent way to capture issues, prioritize work, plan cycles, and connect delivery work to projects. It is less obviously suited to organizations whose core process depends on highly customized forms, extensive approval chains, or portfolio-level resource planning. Before choosing it, write down the workflows the team uses every week and identify where the tool's conventions match or conflict with them.

content.title: Issue Tracking and Planning
content.body: Evaluate how the team creates and triages issues, assigns ownership, sets priorities, manages cycles, and connects issues to projects or milestones. Check whether the available views answer the questions the team actually asks during planning and review. Use a representative project rather than a blank demo workspace, and test blocked work, changing priorities, recurring tasks, and cross-team dependencies. Verify current feature availability in Linear's documentation.

content.title: Developer Workflow and Integrations
content.body: For engineering teams, the practical value often depends on how issue records connect to repositories, pull requests, commits, chat, and deployment workflows. Test the integration path from an issue to a code change and back to the issue status. Confirm which actions happen automatically, which require user input, and how errors are surfaced. Integrations reduce some coordination, but teams still need clear branch, review, release, and ownership conventions.

content.title: Customization and Reporting
content.body: A streamlined workflow may reduce configuration overhead, but it can be a limitation when teams need nonstandard statuses, custom fields, detailed approval paths, or reporting across different operating models. List the reports managers and stakeholders need, then check whether those reports can be produced without exporting data to spreadsheets or maintaining a parallel system. If teams use different definitions of ready, blocked, or complete, agree on those definitions before configuring the workspace.

content.title: Adoption and Administration
content.body: A successful rollout depends on whether engineers, product managers, and stakeholders can maintain the workflow without a dedicated person constantly repairing it. Define issue-writing standards, ownership expectations, cycle planning habits, and where decisions are documented. Test permissions for contractors and cross-functional partners. Assign an administrator who can maintain integrations and workspace conventions, but avoid creating unnecessary rules before the team has run real work through the system.

content.title: Migration and Exit Planning
content.body: Before migrating, map existing statuses, labels, teams, projects, relationships, attachments, and historical records to the destination. Run a small import and verify that users can still find the issues and context they need. Identify reports or automations that rely on the old system's field names. Confirm the available export format and what happens to records if the organization later changes tools. Keep the old system accessible until the team accepts the migrated data.

content.title: Pricing and Plan Verification
content.body: Do not make a decision from an old price table or an assumed feature list. Check Linear's current official pricing and plan documentation for seat limits, collaboration options, administrative controls, support, and any feature the team considers mandatory. Model the cost for the actual team and expected growth, including setup and migration. A low starting cost is not useful if the selected plan cannot support the required workflow.

content.title: Practical Recommendation
content.body: Pilot Linear with one real team and a clearly bounded workflow. Agree on acceptance criteria such as successful issue-to-code linking, understandable planning views, reliable ownership, and reports that answer recurring questions. Compare the experience with the current process and record what remains manual. Choose Linear when its focused model supports the work with fewer workarounds; shortlist a more configurable system when customization, portfolio reporting, or non-engineering workflows are central requirements.

faqs.question: Is Linear only for software engineering teams?
faqs.answer: It is primarily associated with issue tracking and product-development workflows. Other teams may use it, but should test whether its conventions and reporting fit their work.

faqs.question: Can Linear replace a highly customized project management system?
faqs.answer: It depends on the workflows involved. Map required fields, approvals, dependencies, reports, and integrations, then verify them in a pilot before migrating.

faqs.question: Does Linear integrate with developer tools?
faqs.answer: Linear offers developer-workflow integrations, but exact capabilities can change. Verify the current official documentation and test the repository workflow your team uses.

faqs.question: How much does Linear cost?
faqs.answer: Pricing and included features can change. Check Linear's official pricing page for current plans, seat rules, and any features required by your team.

faqs.question: What should a team test before adopting Linear?
faqs.answer: Test issue triage, cycle planning, project reporting, repository integration, permissions, migration, and exporting records if you later switch tools.

author: PilotStack Editorial Team
learningCurve: Steep — requires dedicated training time for full proficiency
whoShouldUse: Linear is designed for fast-growing startups that need a scalable project management platform. Its generous free tier and flexible pricing make it accessible for early-stage companies.
whoShouldNotUse: Linear may be overwhelming for users who only need basic project management functionality. Its extensive feature set can create unnecessary complexity for simple use cases.
